title: Rantideva's last cup of water
hookLine: a king finally sits down to eat after a long fast, and the guests keep coming
carry: seva: work offered, its fruit given away
tomorrow: rain, a tiny shelter, three strangers, and then a fourth.

cards: The plate is finally in front of him. King Rantideva and his family have gone without food for a long time, and now there's a little rice, a little ghee, some water. He lifts his hand to eat.
A knock. A hungry guest. The king shares.
Another knock, another guest. He shares again. Then a man arrives with his dogs, all of them hungry.
Today's summit sit climbs back to the lineage track, and the stretch on karma and seva: work, and work given away.

teach.h: THE LAST OF THE WATER, GIVEN.
teach.b: Here's how the Bhagavata finishes the story, in paraphrase. The king gives the man with the dogs everything that's left, and bows to him and to the dogs. Only the water remains.
Then one more person comes, an outcaste by the rules of the day, thirsty, asking for a drink. The king gives him the water and says something.
He doesn't want great powers from God, he says, and doesn't even ask to be freed from rebirth. He asks to enter the sorrow of all beings and carry it, so they can be free of it.
Then the story turns: the guests were gods come to test him. They show themselves, and he asks them for nothing. Hold that next to the rest of the track.

teach.h: THE BOWL SNATCHED, NO ONE BLAMED.
teach.b: In the Uddhava Gita, a wandering beggar has his bowl snatched away, and he blames no one, not people, not the gods, not even karma, only the grip of his own mind.

teach.h: DO THE WORK, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says the true renouncer isn't the one who quits his work and lets the fire go out, but the one who does the needed work without leaning on what it brings back. And seva: service, offered as worship.
Karma isn't just a ledger of what comes back to you.

teach.h: SEVA: WORK WHOSE FRUIT GOES TO ANOTHER.
teach.b: It's work done without clutching the result, and seva is that work when the result goes to someone else.

Rantideva's meal fed a guest, a stranger, a man with dogs and a thirsty outcaste, and when the gods stood before him, he had nothing left to ask for. It's why many Hindu temples cook and serve free meals and call it seva.

how: Hindus practice seva in many forms: cooking and serving food at temples, caring for the sick and elderly, or working in the community, offered as service to God rather than for reward.

o: a feast a king throws to celebrate his victories
a look back from the top at karma and seva, work given away
a fast kept until the gods grant you a kingdom

games.q: work, given away — tap the pairs.
p: gave his last water to a thirsty outcaste
blamed only the grip of his own mind
does the work, lets go of the fruit

s: in the story, Rantideva eats first and gives away the leftovers
he gives before he eats: to each guest in turn, until only the water is left, and then the water.
Rantideva asks to carry the sorrow of all beings so they can be free
he asks neither for powers nor for his own release from rebirth.
in the Gita, the true renouncer is the one who quits all work
Krishna says it's the one who does the work that needs doing, without leaning on its fruit.

games.q: you're Rantideva. only a cup of water is left, and a thirsty outcaste asks for a drink. what do you do?
o: drink it, since you've already given everything else.
games.why: the king gives him the water, and asks not for powers or release, but to carry the sorrow of all beings.

practice: Bring to mind one ordinary piece of work you'll do today, a shift, a meal, a report, a ride for someone.

On an out-breath, let your shoulders drop as if setting down what it will bring you, the thanks, the credit, the result; keep the work, let the fruit go, and if you pray, offer the work to God before you begin.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today: karma and seva, and a king who gave away his last cup of water. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi, in Devanagari: sevā, service, offered as worship.

carryVoice: Your line: seva is work offered to God, its fruit given away. The work stays in your hands. Rest well.
